title: Practical 2: Population genetic models and simulations
text:
Effective population size (Ne)
In the Wright-Fisher model every individual has the same chance of contributing offspring. In nature this is not the case. The effective population size (Ne) is the size of an ideal population that would have equally strong drift (lose diversity equally fast) as ours. In an ideal population Ne = Nc (number of adults). In nature Ne is almost always much smaller: often around 10% of Nc (Frankham 1995), and 2.5–5% in eagles from Norway and Iceland (Hansen et al. 2023).






PomembnoN is not Ne



N (or Nc) is the number of individuals we count. Ne tells us how quickly a population loses diversity. Two populations with the same number of individuals can have very different Ne if they differ in sex ratio, reproductive success or size history.



How we measure Ne
We cannot count Ne, but we can measure it by its effect. Because He decreases each generation by a factor of \((1 - \frac{1}{2N_e})\), log(He) against generation is a straight line with slope log(1 − 1/2Ne). The function estimate_ne() measures this slope and calculates Ne from it:

estimate_ne <- function(He, generation) {
  slope <- coef(lm(log(He) ~ generation))[["generation"]]   # slope of the line log(He) ~ generation
  1 / (2 * (1 - exp(slope)))                               # calculate Ne from the slope
}

In Practical 6 we will estimate Ne the same way from real data (historical versus contemporary eagles).


Sex ratio
What we want to show. That an unequal sex ratio reduces Ne, even with the same number of individuals.
Parameters. Always 100 adults: 50 males and 50 females, 20 and 80, and 5 and 95. According to the formula
\[N_e = \frac{4 N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}\]
In each generation we randomly draw the genes of the breeding males and females; the offspring get half of their genes from fathers and half from mothers. We simulate 1000 independent loci at once (the vector p), measure He and finally calculate Ne with estimate_ne().

simulate_sexes <- function(N_m, N_f, generations = 50, loci = 1000) {
  p  <- rep(0.5, loci)                          # allele frequency at each locus
  He <- mean(2 * p * (1 - p))
  for (t in 1:generations) {
    p_males   <- rbinom(loci, 2 * N_m, p) / (2 * N_m)   # genes of the N_m breeding males
    p_females <- rbinom(loci, 2 * N_f, p) / (2 * N_f)   # genes of the N_f females
    p <- (p_males + p_females) / 2              # offspring: half of their genes from fathers, half from mothers
    He <- c(He, mean(2 * p * (1 - p)))          # store mean He
  }
  tibble(generation = 0:generations, He = He)
}

s1 <- simulate_sexes(50, 50)
s2 <- simulate_sexes(20, 80)
s3 <- simulate_sexes(5, 95)

tibble(males      = c(50, 20, 5),
       females    = c(50, 80, 95),
       formula    = 4 * males * females / (males + females),
       simulation = c(estimate_ne(s1$He, s1$generation), estimate_ne(s2$He, s2$generation), estimate_ne(s3$He, s3$generation)))

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  males females formula simulation
  <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
1    50      50     100       99.5
2    20      80      64       61.7
3     5      95      19       18.4


Interpretation. The column formula is Ne from the formula, simulation Ne measured from the rate of loss of He. They agree (the simulation is random, so not exactly). With five males a population of 100 loses diversity as fast as an ideal population of only about 19: half of the genes of each generation come from just five males.


Differences in reproductive success
Even with equal numbers of the sexes, Ne is reduced when a few individuals produce most of the offspring:
\[N_e \approx \frac{4N - 2}{V_k + 2}\]
where Vk is the variance in the number of offspring per individual (on average each individual has 2 offspring). In an ideal population Vk ≈ 2 and Ne ≈ N. With N = 100 and Vk = 18 (a few individuals have many offspring, most none), Ne ≈ 20.






OpombaQuestion



In Iceland in 2022, 92 territorial pairs fledged only 38 chicks (Hansen et al. 2023). What does this mean for Vk and Ne? Why can Ne in eagles be much smaller than the number of pairs, even though eagles are monogamous?




Fluctuating population size
What we want to show. That a short period of small size strongly reduces the long-term Ne.
If the size changes, Ne over t generations is approximately the harmonic mean of the sizes:
\[N_e \approx \frac{t}{\sum_{i=1}^{t} 1/N_i}\]

sizes <- c(rep(500, 10), rep(20, 2), rep(500, 10))   # 10 generations of 500, 2 of 20, 10 of 500
c(arithmetic = mean(sizes),
  harmonic   = length(sizes) / sum(1 / sizes))

arithmetic   harmonic 
  456.3636   157.1429 


Interpretation. The population had on average 456 individuals, but its Ne is only 157: two generations with 20 individuals reduced it to a third. The harmonic mean is very sensitive to small values.
Parameters of the next plot. The population starts with 20 individuals and grows to about 300 in 27 generations, similar to the eagles in Iceland after protection. For each generation we calculate Ne as the harmonic mean of all sizes up to that generation.

growth <- tibble(generation = 0:27,
                 N = round(20 * exp(0.1 * generation))) |>   # exponential growth from 20 to ~300
  mutate(Ne = (generation + 1) / cumsum(1 / N))              # harmonic mean up to each generation

growth |>
  pivot_longer(c(N, Ne), names_to = "size", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(generation, value, colour = size)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(N = "#B5542C", Ne = "#1F5FA8"),
                      labels = c(N = "actual size (N)", Ne = "effective size (Ne)")) +
  labs(x = "generation", y = "population size", colour = NULL)







Slika 7.6: A rapidly growing population (red) and its Ne as the harmonic mean of all past sizes (blue). After Figure 5.7 in Jobling et al. (2013).





Interpretation. The population grew more than tenfold, but Ne barely changed. Today’s genetic diversity is a consequence of past small size. We therefore distinguish the long-term Ne (determines today’s diversity) from the recent Ne (how strong drift we can expect in the future).






OpombaQuestion



The Danish eagle population went extinct at the beginning of the 20th century and was recolonised in 1995; in 2020 it had 133 pairs. Norway has about 2000 pairs. Which has the higher long-term Ne? Does it matter where the first pairs came from?

title: Practical 2: Population genetic models and simulations
text:
Bottleneck and founder effect
Two events reduce diversity faster than ordinary drift:

a bottleneck: a large population is strongly reduced for a few generations and then grows again,
a founder effect: a new population is founded by a small number of individuals (e.g. colonisation of an island).

To see the loss of rare alleles we need a locus with many alleles (a SNP has only two). We take a locus with 20 alleles: a few common and many rare.

freq0 <- 0.8^(0:19)                   # 20 alleles with decreasing frequency
freq0 <- freq0 / sum(freq0)           # frequencies must sum to 1
round(freq0, 3)

 [1] 0.202 0.162 0.129 0.104 0.083 0.066 0.053 0.042 0.034 0.027 0.022 0.017
[13] 0.014 0.011 0.009 0.007 0.006 0.005 0.004 0.003

c(richness = 20, He = 1 - sum(freq0^2))

 richness        He 
20.000000  0.886297 



Bottleneck
What we want to show. That a bottleneck reduces allelic richness much more than He.
Parameters. 10 generations with N = 2000, 5 generations with N = 10 (bottleneck), then 30 generations with N = 2000; 200 replicates.

one_population <- function(sizes, freq0) {
  f <- freq0
  richness <- numeric(length(sizes))
  He <- numeric(length(sizes))
  for (t in seq_along(sizes)) {
    N <- sizes[t]
    copies <- rmultinom(1, size = 2 * N, prob = f)   # how many of the 2N copies are of each of the 20 alleles
    f <- as.vector(copies) / (2 * N)                  # new allele frequencies
    richness[t] <- sum(f > 0)                         # how many alleles are still present
    He[t] <- 1 - sum(f^2)
  }
  tibble(generation = seq_along(sizes), richness = richness, He = He)
}

sizes <- c(rep(2000, 10), rep(10, 5), rep(2000, 30))
replicates <- bind_rows(replicate(200, one_population(sizes, freq0), simplify = FALSE))

bottleneck <- replicates |>
  group_by(generation) |>
  summarise(richness = mean(richness) / 20,                # proportion of the starting richness (20 alleles)
            He       = mean(He) / (1 - sum(freq0^2)))      # proportion of the starting He

bottleneck |>
  pivot_longer(-generation, names_to = "measure", values_to = "proportion") |>
  ggplot(aes(generation, proportion, colour = measure)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 10.5, xmax = 15.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(richness = "#B5542C", He = "#1F5FA8"),
                      labels = c(richness = "allelic richness", He = "He")) +
  labs(x = "generation", y = "proportion of starting value", colour = NULL)







Slika 7.7: Bottleneck: 10 generations with N = 2000, 5 generations with N = 10 (grey), then 30 generations with N = 2000. Both measures are shown as a proportion of the starting value (mean of 200 replicates).





Interpretation. The y axis is the proportion of the starting value (1 = as much as at the start); the grey band is the bottleneck. During the bottleneck allelic richness drops to about a quarter, but He only to about three quarters. Rare alleles easily fail to appear in a small sample (20 copies), but they contribute almost nothing to He. After the bottleneck the population grows, but diversity does not come back: new alleles can only arise by mutation or migration. This is why allelic richness is a good indicator of a recent bottleneck.


Founder effect
What we want to show. How much of the source population’s diversity k founders take with them.
Parameters. k = 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 or 50 founders (2k gene copies), drawn at random from the source population with frequencies freq0; each number is repeated 1000 times. We simulate only the moment of founding.

founding <- function(k) {
  alleles <- sample(1:20, size = 2 * k, replace = TRUE, prob = freq0)   # 2k gene copies of the founders
  f <- table(alleles) / (2 * k)                                         # allele frequencies in the new population
  c(richness = length(f) / 20,                                          # proportion of the 20 source alleles
    He = (1 - sum(f^2)) / (1 - sum(freq0^2)))                           # proportion of the source He
}

k_values <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)
means <- sapply(k_values, function(k) rowMeans(replicate(1000, founding(k))))   # mean of 1000 replicates for each k
founders <- tibble(k = k_values, richness = means["richness", ], He = means["He", ])

founders |>
  pivot_longer(-k, names_to = "measure", values_to = "proportion") |>
  ggplot(aes(k, proportion, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(richness = "#B5542C", He = "#1F5FA8"),
                      labels = c(richness = "allelic richness", He = "He")) +
  labs(x = "number of founders (k)", y = "proportion of source diversity", colour = NULL)







Slika 7.8: Proportion of the allelic richness and He of the source population retained by k founders (mean of 1000 replicates).





Interpretation. The x axis is the number of founders (log scale), the y axis the proportion of the source population’s diversity. Already 5 founders retain about 90% of He (expected \(1 - \frac{1}{2k}\)), but only about a third of the alleles; even 50 founders retain only about four fifths. Retaining rare alleles requires very many founders.






OpombaQuestion



Iceland and Greenland were colonised by eagles from the mainland. Which measure of diversity would you expect to be lower on the islands: allelic richness or He? Can a population lose many alleles without He changing much?

title: Practical 2: Population genetic models and simulations
text:
Migration and gene flow
Drift acts independently in each population, so isolated populations become more and more different. Migration (gene flow) brings alleles from other populations and reduces the differences. In each generation a proportion m of individuals are immigrants from the other population:
\[p_1' = (1 - m)\,p_1 + m\,p_2\]

Migration equalises frequencies
What we want to show. How quickly migration equalises two different populations when there is no drift.
Parameters. p1 = 0.9 and p2 = 0.1; m = 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1; 50 generations; very large populations (no drift).

convergence <- function(m, generations = 50) {
  p1 <- 0.9; p2 <- 0.1
  for (t in 1:generations) {
    p1_new <- (1 - m) * p1[t] + m * p2[t]      # part of population 1 is replaced by immigrants from 2
    p2_new <- (1 - m) * p2[t] + m * p1[t]      # and vice versa
    p1 <- c(p1, p1_new); p2 <- c(p2, p2_new)
  }
  tibble(m = m, generation = 0:generations, p1 = p1, p2 = p2)
}

bind_rows(convergence(0.01), convergence(0.05), convergence(0.1)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(p1, p2), names_to = "population", values_to = "p") |>
  ggplot(aes(generation, p, colour = population)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("m =", m)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(p1 = "#B5542C", p2 = "#1F5FA8")) +
  labs(x = "generation", y = "allele frequency", colour = NULL)







Slika 7.9: Allele frequencies in two populations exchanging a proportion m of individuals per generation (no drift). The dashed line is the overall mean of 0.5.





Interpretation. Each panel is one migration rate. The difference between the populations shrinks each generation by a factor of (1 − 2m). With m = 0.1 the frequencies become equal in about 20 generations; with m = 0.01 they are still quite different after 50 generations. Because there is no drift, this is deterministic: every run gives the same plot.


Drift versus migration: FST
What we want to show. That drift pushes populations apart while migration brings them together, and how we measure this with FST.
We measure differentiation with FST, which compares the heterozygosity within populations (HS) with that of the pooled population (HT):
\[F_{ST} = \frac{H_T - H_S}{H_T}\]
Parameters. Two populations of N = 50, both starting at p = 0.5 at 500 loci (FST = 0); each generation first migration (m), then drift; m = 0, 0.002, 0.02 and 0.1; 200 generations.

fst_over_time <- function(m, N = 50, generations = 200, loci = 500) {
  p1 <- rep(0.5, loci); p2 <- rep(0.5, loci)          # frequencies at all loci in both populations
  FST <- numeric(generations)
  for (t in 1:generations) {
    p1_m <- (1 - m) * p1 + m * p2                     # 1. migration
    p2_m <- (1 - m) * p2 + m * p1
    p1 <- rbinom(loci, 2 * N, p1_m) / (2 * N)         # 2. drift in each population separately
    p2 <- rbinom(loci, 2 * N, p2_m) / (2 * N)
    HS <- mean((2 * p1 * (1 - p1) + 2 * p2 * (1 - p2)) / 2)   # mean He within populations
    p_total <- (p1 + p2) / 2
    HT <- mean(2 * p_total * (1 - p_total))                   # He of the pooled population
    FST[t] <- (HT - HS) / HT
  }
  tibble(m = m, generation = 1:generations, FST = FST)
}

bind_rows(fst_over_time(0), fst_over_time(0.002), fst_over_time(0.02), fst_over_time(0.1)) |>
  mutate(m = paste0("m = ", m, " (Nm = ", 50 * m, ")")) |>
  ggplot(aes(generation, FST, colour = m)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "generation", y = expression(F[ST]), colour = NULL)







Slika 7.10: FST between two populations of N = 50 for different proportions of immigrants per generation (m). Nm is the number of immigrants per generation.





Interpretation. Each line is one migration rate; FST = 0 means identical populations, 1 fixation for different alleles. Without migration FST keeps increasing. With migration it settles where drift and migration are in balance. Even one immigrant per generation (Nm = 1) strongly limits differentiation. In the island model the equilibrium is approximately \(F_{ST} \approx \frac{1}{4Nm + 1}\).






PomembnoA common misinterpretation



FST measures differentiation; it is not a direct measure of the number of migrants. The formula \(F_{ST} \approx 1/(4Nm + 1)\) holds only under very simplified assumptions (island model, equilibrium, no selection or mutation). Migration also does not always increase diversity within a population: it does so only if immigrants bring different alleles.








OpombaQuestion



There are no reports of migrants between Greenland, Iceland and the mainland (Hansen et al. 2023). What FST between Iceland and Norway would you expect? You will check your answer in Practical 5.
